newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Third Australian dies under suicide law.
newsitem.headline: Third Australian dies under suicide law.

text.p: A 69-year-old man has become the third Australian to commit suicide under the euthanasia law of the remote Northern Territory, a euthanasia supporters group said on Wednesday.

The National Coalition for Voluntary Euthanasia said on its Internet site that the man, who had asked not to be named, had been suffering from terminal stomach cancer and died on Monday using a computerised lethal injection system.
The man's death follows those of fellow cancer patients Bob Dent, 66, and Janet Mills, 52, who used the Northern Territory's law to end their lives in September and on January 2 respectively.
A spokesman for the National Coalition for Voluntary Euthanasia, Dr Robert Marr, said the latest death showed that medical specialists were becoming more comfortable using the controversial law.
Mills held a news conference in early December in order to plea for a specialist to come forward to supply the approval she needed.

"The specialist was very happy to sign the form (for the latest death) and all the safeguards have been met and it shows the law is working well," Marr told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio on Wednesday.
"I think from now there are no problems with the law.

"Other doctors are coming forward to help (euthanasia campaigner) Dr (Philip) Nitschke and although we do not expect many people to be using the law -- at the most one a month -- dying patients at last have the right to be able to choose voluntary euthanasia if their suffering becomes too great."
Under the law, a terminally ill person needs the signatures of a doctor, a psychiatrist and a specialist before going ahead with the procedure.
Following Mills' death, it was disclosed that the specialist did not need to be resident in the Northern Territory as was previously thought.
The world's first euthanasia law came into effect in July last year in the lightly-populated outback region of the Northern Territory.

It sparked an outcry from some doctors as well as church and Aboriginal leaders and the Federal parliament is currently considering a bill to overturn the territory law, which it has the constitutional power to do.

The lower house of Federal parliament, the House of Representatives, passed the law in December. A parliamentary committee will inquire into it before the upper house, the Senate, votes on the bill later this year.
The outcome of the Senate vote is uncertain.
